chunks: "At 100 percent duty the high-side switch never turns off.

The switch node sits at the input voltage minus a small drop, the inductor has a constant DC voltage across it, so there's no ripple, and the output is just the input minus the drops across the switch and inductor resistance.
Nothing is regulating anymore; the converter is acting as a low-resistance pass element. That's dropout. For 2 amps through 110 milliohms, the output is about 0.
Practically, a high-side NFET driven with a bootstrap capacitor can't stay on forever, because the bootstrap cap is only recharged when the switch node goes low, and it slowly drains.
So controllers have a minimum off-time or a periodic refresh pulse, which limits the maximum duty to maybe 95 to 99 percent, unless there's a charge pump or a PMOS high-side.
At 0 percent the high-side is off all the time. The inductor sees minus V out so its current ramps down to zero at V out over L .
In a diode or diode-emulating converter it stops at zero and the output decays through the load.
In a forced-PWM synchronous converter the current continues negative, so the output capacitor pushes energy back into the input, which can raise the input voltage if nothing sinks it.
In both cases the loop is saturated, so regulation is lost."
